teaser: A god offers you wine with dirty fingernails. Would you take the glass?
review_notes:
Date: catalog says 1596; usually dated c. 1596-1598.
Rediscovered in the Uffizi storerooms in 1913 (attribution to Caravaggio published by Roberto Longhi/Matteo Marangoni shortly after).
Tiny self-portrait reflected in the carafe: noticed after a 1922 cleaning, confirmed by reflectography in 2009; it is not legible in this image, the spot text says so.
Gift from Cardinal Del Monte to Grand Duke Ferdinando I de' Medici.
Model often identified as Mario Minniti (hypothesis).
Use of a mirror explaining the glass held in the left hand is a hypothesis and is presented as such.
Size about 95 x 85 cm.

lesson.text: Would you take the glass? He is holding it out to you, after all. A wide, shallow goblet, filled to the brim with dark red wine, pushed across the table toward the exact spot where you are standing. Before you answer, it is worth finding out who is offering, and what state the drink is in.

Officially, this is Bacchus, the Roman god of wine, crowned with vine leaves and grapes. Painters had shown him for centuries as an ideal youth with marble skin. Caravaggio, about 25 and newly arrived in a cardinal's household in Rome, takes the same subject and does something nobody expected. He paints the model.

lesson.title: A god, or a boy from the street?
lesson.text: Check the evidence, starting with the head.

spots.title: The face
spots.text: Cheeks flushed pink, eyelids heavy, a thick black mass of hair that looks very much like a wig. He seems a little drunk already, and slightly bored with posing.

spots.title: The hand
spots.text: Red and weathered, far darker than the arm above it. This is the hand of someone who works outdoors. The fingernails have dark rims of dirt under them.

spots.title: The body
spots.text: The chest and shoulder are pale and soft, where clothes normally cover them. Tanned face and hands, white torso: the tan lines of a working boy undressed for the occasion.

spots.title: The couch
spots.text: Under the white sheet, a blue-striped cushion pokes out: ordinary mattress ticking. The ancient banquet couch is a studio daybed with linen thrown over it.

lesson.text: So the costume is thin, and Caravaggio wants you to see through it. That was the scandal and the charm of his early pictures: gods and saints played by recognizable Romans, with their sunburn and their grime left in. The model here may be his friend Mario Minniti, a young Sicilian painter who shared his lodgings.

The patron was Cardinal Francesco Maria Del Monte, a cultured churchman who housed Caravaggio in his palace, fed him and paid him a salary. Del Monte sent this Bacchus to Florence as a diplomatic gift for the Grand Duke of Tuscany, Ferdinando de' Medici.

Now back to that glass. A painting is a still thing, and this one seems calmer than most: a boy leaning on an elbow, nothing happening. But Caravaggio has slipped a tiny event into it, a sign that time is passing while you look. It concerns the wine.
Something in this quiet picture is moving. Can you find it?

spots.title: Ripples
spots.text: Fine rings spread across the surface of the wine in the goblet. The hand holding the stem is not quite steady, or the glass has only just been filled. He cannot hold this pose forever.

lesson.text: Those rings are a small marvel of observation, and they change the mood. An unsteady hand, a full glass held by a thin stem between fingertips: the offer will not last. There is a second sign of it at the far left, where bubbles still cling to the edge of the wine in the big carafe, as if it had been set down seconds ago.

He holds the goblet in his left hand, which is unusual for a toast. One explanation is that Caravaggio worked from a reflection in a mirror, which flips left and right. Nobody can prove it, but an early biographer did say he painted some of his first pictures with the help of a mirror.
Caravaggio paints the instant, never the eternal. Even a god gets a trembling glass, a flushed cheek and a pose that is about to end.

And then there is the fruit. On the cardinal's table it should be perfect, the sort of display that shows off a painter's skill. Caravaggio does show off. Every grape has its bloom and every leaf its veins. But he selected this basket with a certain cruelty. Go through it.

spots.title: The apple
spots.text: A red and yellow apple with a dark wormhole bored into its skin. The first thing your eye meets in the basket is already inhabited.

spots.title: A bruised fruit
spots.text: This golden fruit carries a spreading brown patch of rot. Caravaggio renders the decay as lovingly as the healthy skin next to it.

spots.title: The pomegranate
spots.text: Split wide open, spilling its red seeds. It is overripe, at the point where fruit bursts on its own.

spots.title: Dying leaves
spots.text: Dry, curling leaves hang over the edge of the dish, yellow and brown. The season in this basket is late autumn, well past the harvest.

spots.title: The crown
spots.text: The same story on his head: among the green vine leaves, several have turned yellow and rust red. The wreath is wilting as he wears it.

spots.title: The black bow
spots.text: With his free hand he toys with the dark ribbon that ties his robe, as if about to undo it. The invitation may be to more than a drink.

spots.title: The carafe
spots.text: Restorers found a minute reflection on this glass: a figure at an easel, taken to be Caravaggio himself at work. It is far too small to make out here, but it is in the real painting.

lesson.text: Rotting fruit beside a beautiful boy is a message viewers of the time read easily. Pleasure is sweet and short. Youth, wine and ripe pears all spoil on the same schedule. Art historians call this kind of reminder a vanitas, from the Latin for “emptiness.” Caravaggio delivers it without a single skull, only a fruit bowl.

In Florence the picture was eventually forgotten. It lay unframed in the Uffizi's storerooms until 1913, when it was pulled out, dirty and unattributed, and recognized soon after as a Caravaggio. It measures only about 95 by 85 cm (37 by 33 inches).

So, the glass. You now know the wine is trembling, the fruit is turning, the wreath is drying and the god is a tired boy with dirty nails who would like to stop posing. Oddly, that makes the offer more tempting. He is saying: this will not keep. Take it now.

quiz.question: What detail in the goblet shows that time is passing?
options: Ripples on the surface of the wine
quiz.explanation: Fine rings spread across the wine, as if the hand were unsteady.

quiz.question: What gives the “god” away as a real working boy?
options: Sunburned hands with dirty nails and a pale torso
quiz.explanation: His hands and face are tanned and his nails dirty, while his chest is pale.

quiz.question: What is wrong with the fruit in the basket?
options: It is all unripe and green
Much of it is wormy, bruised or overripe
quiz.explanation: A wormhole, a rotten patch and a burst pomegranate show it is past its best.

quiz.question: Who sent this painting to Florence as a gift?
quiz.explanation: Del Monte, Caravaggio's patron, gave it to the Grand Duke of Tuscany.

quiz.question: What does a vanitas remind the viewer of?
options: That pleasure and youth do not last
That wine is a gift of the gods
quiz.explanation: A vanitas points to the shortness of life and its pleasures.

quiz.question: What did restorers find reflected in the carafe?
options: A tiny figure at an easel
quiz.explanation: A minute reflection of a painter at work, taken to be Caravaggio.

facts.text: The painting spent years forgotten in the Uffizi's storerooms.
Bacchus rests on a carved marble throne.
facts.explanation: He leans on a daybed: a striped mattress cushion shows under the sheet.

facts.text: All the leaves in his crown are fresh and green.
facts.explanation: Several have turned yellow and red; the wreath is wilting.
